newsitem.title: BAHRAIN: FEATURE-Bahrain economy seen recovering next year.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Bahrain economy seen recovering next year.

text.p: Bahrain's economy, slowed in recent years by weak oil prices and civil unrest, is set to take off next year with several development projects in the pipeline, officials, economists and diplomats said.

They said the allocation of the entire production of a joint offshore oilfield with Saudi Arabia, higher oil prices and various construction projects would significantly contribute to the small Gulf Arab state's economic recovery.
"Lower oil prices in the world market and developments in the region including the 1991 Gulf War had slowed down Bahrain's economic recovery," an economist told Reuters.
"But the economy is starting to recover. Prospects indicate there will be some improvement next year," he added.

Official figures show gross domestic product (GDP) in real terms rose 2.3 percent in 1994 after rising 8.2 percent in 1993. Official 1995 figures have not yet been released, but Commerce Minister Ali Saleh Abdullah al-Saleh said in June GDP grew 4.2 percent in the year. It was not clear if he was referring to real or nominal growth.

Henry Azzam, chief economist at Saudi Arabia's National Commercial Bank, estimates growth in Bahrain slowed last year to about 0.5 percent from 3.2 percent in 1994. He forecast GDP growth in Bahrain at 1.5 percent this year.

"I think Bahrain's economy will improve in the next 12 months. Now the government is getting extra revenue from Abu Safa oilfield, it will use that money to balance its budget," a Western diplomat said.

Saudi Arabia agreed this year to allocate the balance of oil production from the field it shares with Bahrain to the small state to help boost its economy and narrow its budget deficit, which the commerce minister in June said was 65.2 million dinars ($173 million) in 1995 from 130.3 million dinars in 1994.
1994 nominal GDP was 1.8 billion dinars.
Analysts said Bahrain started receiving all revenues from the 140,000 barrels per day (bpd) from April 1 which would generate around $200 million a year to the economy.
Bahrain produces some 40,000 bpd from its own fields and imports 200,000 bpd of Saudi crude for refining.

Officials said the least wealthy Gulf Arab state will spend around 900 million dinars in the next five years on development projects including a new $600 million power and water plant, a port and a bridge at a new industrial area in Hidd.

Economists said the effect on the economy of recent protests by members of the Shi'ite Moslem majority seeking political and economic reforms, including jobs, had been mainly in damaging consumer and investor confidence and curbing tourism.
The trade, hotels and restaurants sector is an important one, contributing 11.4 percent to GDP in 1994.

Since the Bahrain-Saudi causeway was built in 1986, more than a dozen hotels have opened and the island has become a regional tourism centre, mainly for Gulf nationals taking advantage of its relaxed social environment.
Economists said the unrest, which included bomb attacks on five hotels this year, had kept some tourists away and had made residents more cautious about spending their money.
"Maybe because of the political uncertainty earlier in the year, maybe the overall weakness of the Gulf economy in the last few years has made them uncertain about prospects," one said.
"People are holding back on investment decisions because of the domestic political situation and also because of the general flat economic performance of the region," a diplomat said.

At least 26 people have been killed since the unrest erupted in December 1994. Recently Bahrain has contained the unrest. But the economy continues to be dogged by unemployment, officially put at 1.4 percent, but which economists see at 10-15 percent.
Officials say they are studying a comprehensive tourism plan and have formed a ministerial committee to review projects to boost economic growth and create jobs for Bahrainis.
Bahrain's Gulf Arab allies are also helping spur growth by linking financial assistance to development projects.
Four funds in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and United Arab Emirates earlier this year gave Bahrain loans worth 26.6 million dinars to finance the expansion of the power distribution network.
Analysts said Bahrain's standing as a regional financial and banking hub had been little affected by the unrest.
"Bahrain will remain a financial centre for the Gulf and the Middle East, but the growth prospects are limited for banking in terms of asset growth," an economist said.
There are 48 offshore banking units with assets of some $67 billion and 19 commercial banks with assets of 2.5 billion dinars operating in Bahrain.
